Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A striped hot air balloon floating over rows of lavender at sunset, with a lone tree on a golden hill

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

11 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The striped balloon, upper left (center 28% across, 15% down in the frame) Light: The setting sun, low and a little left of center (43% across, 41% down in the frame), shining toward the viewer: the balloon's right side, the tree's left side, and the tops of the lavender rows catch the lightHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: blending the whole skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #10 round: cloud shapesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: dry brushing the light edgesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff brush: tapping grassy clumpsOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • old stiff flat or round: dabbing the crownOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • old stiff flat: dabbing the rowsOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #8 round: the light dabsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • Liner (#1 or #0): ropesLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • #4 round: highlightsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8Step 9Step 10Step 11

STEP 1 OF 11

Blend the sunset sky and the sun

  1. The light comes from the sun, low and a little left of center, 37% across and 42% down. Every highlight faces it.
  2. 1 inch flat, creamy Sky blue, side to side across the top 5%.
  3. Below it, Sunset orange with extra red to 25% down, then plain Sunset orange to 35%, blending each into the wet band above.
  4. X strokes of Sun gold from 35% down to a straight, level line at 62%.
  5. #6 round: a Sun cream circle about 3/4 inch wide at 37% across, 42% down, softened into the wet gold around it.
Paints for this step4 paints, 4 new
  • Sky blue new2 parts white, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of red
  • Sunset orange new2 parts yellow, 2 parts red, 1 part white
  • Sun gold new3 parts yellow, 1 part red, 1 part white
  • Sun cream new6 parts white, 2 parts yellow, 1 part red

For the coral band under the blue, add a little extra red to Sunset orange.

Brushes

1 inch flat#6 round

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat side to side across the whole width, overlapping each band's wet edge so the colors melt together.

X stroke. Criss-cross the flat in overlapping X shapes through the gold so it blends with soft texture.

Watch out: Colors dry a little darker, so test each mix on the palette edge first.

Watch out: Don't stop the gold at the hill line: carry it to the straight line at 62% so the hills and lavender go over it.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

No diagram: A gradient: the bands are named in order with where each sits.

STEP 2 OF 11

Paint the coral clouds

  1. Let the sky dry. #10 round, creamy Cloud shadow, small circles for each cloud's bottom: a big mass upper right (50-100% across, top to 22% down), one center (34-56% across, 16-28%), one far left (0-12% across, 10-28%).
  2. Small circles of Cloud coral over each cloud's middle, plus thin streaks across the right half at 28-40% down and two short ones level with the sun, one each side.
  3. Dab Sky blue into the gaps across the top left, between the clouds.
  4. Dry brush Cloud light on the top edges only. Keep the sun itself clear.

Brushes

#10 round1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Small circles. Scrub the brush tip in small overlapping circles so the cloud edge stays bumpy and soft.

Dry brush. Wipe the brush almost dry and skim the top edge lightly so the light color breaks up.

Watch out: Too much paint makes hard blobs: wipe the brush so the edges stay soft.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 11

Paint the far mountains and the lake

  1. Let the sky dry. 1/2 inch flat, creamy Mountain purple, horizontal strokes: a left peak at 5% across and 38% down, a right peak at 62% across and 40% down, dipping to a valley under the sun at 48% down.
  2. Ridge blue in a darker band in front, 46-53% down, across the whole width. While wet, tap its top edge with the flat's corner for a low, bumpy tree line.
  3. #6 round, Sun gold: a thin lake strip from 28% to 50% across, 50-53% down.
  4. Soft mountain edges, no texture. The orange-gold sky still shows below the ridge.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat#6 round

Strokes

Horizontal strokes for flat ground. Keep the flat level and the strokes long; follow the mountain's top line with the flat edge, then fill down.

Watch out: Keep the mountain tops below the sun: the sun sits just above the valley.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 11

Paint the golden hills

  1. Let the mountains dry. 1 inch flat, Hill olive, long curved strokes along the slopes: the left hill from the left edge to the center, top at 52% down.
  2. The right hill rises from 30% across at 61% down to a crest at 46% down from 80% across to the right edge.
  3. While wet, sweep Hill gold along the tops, following the slope and blending into the olive. Carry both down to 63%.
  4. Once it sets a little, tap small Hill olive clumps over the lower slopes with an old stiff brush, fewer near the tops.

  • Hill gold new1 part yellow, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of red, a touch of white
  • Hill olive new3 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

Brushes

1 inch flatold stiff brush

Strokes

Curved strokes that follow a form. Sweep the flat along each hill's slope, so the marks bend with the ground.

Wet-on-wet blend. Lay the gold into the wet olive with a light touch, and stop as soon as it drags.

Dabbing. Tap the corner of the stiff brush with a little olive, so the clumps stay broken and the gold shows between them.

Watch out: Work fast and stop blending when the paint starts to drag.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 11

Paint the lone tree

  1. Let the hills dry. #6 round, Trunk brown, press and lift: the trunk at 86-88% across, from the crest at 46% down up to 40%, forking into a Y as in the diagram.
  2. Old stiff brush, Tree dark green, dabbing: a lumpy round crown from 75% to 98% across, 21-42% down.
  3. Dab Tree green over the middle, then a few Tree light green dabs on the left side, toward the sun. Dark green stays on the right and underneath.
  4. Dab a thin, bumpy strip of Tree dark green along the crest from the trunk to the right edge: the tree's shadow on the grass.
Build the depth, dark first

Brushes

#6 roundold stiff flat or round

Strokes

Press and lift. Press the round down at the base of the trunk and lift as you pull up, so it tapers into the branches.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff brush with little paint; dark everywhere first, then lighter dabs on the lit side.

Watch out: Keep the crown lumpy, not a smooth ball.

Watch out: Try a few dabs on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 11

Block in the lavender rows and paths

  1. Dot the vanishing point 58% across and 61% down (8.1 in from the left, 6.7 in down).
  2. 1/2 inch flat, Path orange, strokes toward the dot: two straight paths to the bottom edge, the left ending at 26-38% across, the right at 72-83%.
  3. 1 inch flat, creamy Lavender dark: fill the rest of the field from 61% down, every stroke along a row toward the dot.
  4. Let it dry. 1/2 inch flat on its edge, Row shadow: about five lines each side fanning from the dot as in the diagram, a finger wide in front, thin near the dot.
Paints for this step3 paints, 3 new
  • Lavender dark new3 parts ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white
  • Row shadow new3 parts ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow, a touch of white
  • Path orange new3 parts red, 3 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts white, 1 part yellow

Brushes

1 inch flat1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Strokes toward a vanishing point. Start each stroke at the bottom edge and pull it toward the dot, so the rows are wide in front and thin at the back.

Watch out: Check each path and row line with the brush handle held from the dot: they're straight, not curved.

Watch out: It looks flat and odd right now. That's the ugly stage, and it's normal.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 11

Dab the lavender bodies

  1. Let the field dry. Old stiff flat, lightly loaded with Lavender mid: flick quick upward strokes from the base of each row so each tuft tapers to a point, across the whole field.
  2. Big tufts in the front rows (about 1 inch), small and close near the dot. Let them overlap the path edges a little.
  3. Lavender dark and the Row shadow gaps still show at each row's base.
Paints for this step1 paint, 1 new
  • Lavender mid new3 parts ultramarine, 2 parts white, 1 part red

Brushes

old stiff flat

Strokes

Flicking. Start at the row's base and flick up and off quickly with little paint, so each tuft has a broken, pointed tip.

Watch out: Do every row a little at a time, not one corner to a finish.

Watch out: Test a few dabs on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

Dab the light lavender tops

  3. Most of the mid purple still shows.

STEP 9 OF 11

Paint the balloon's stripes

  1. Let the sky dry. #8 round, Balloon blue: outline the balloon from 11% to 29% across and 3% to 27% down (2.5 in wide, 2.6 in tall), built as in the diagram.
  2. #6 round, curved strokes top to bottom, stripes left to right: blue, red, yellow, blue (widest, center), red, yellow, blue, Sunset orange, yellow.
  3. Bow each stripe with the balloon's curve, all meeting at top and bottom. Flat color, no shading yet; two coats where sky shows through.

Before starting

Subject: A striped hot air balloon over a lavender field at sunset, with a lone tree on a golden hill

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No screen, page, or border around it.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: the left 11% (cloud and field) and the right 4% (cloud and hill)

Why: The picture is 3:2 and the canvas 14:11; a crop keeps the balloon, sun, tree, and rows whole.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: yes, a village of houses and cypresses, plus bushes along the hills. Textures of hundreds of items: yes, every lavender stalk. Detail inside big shapes: yes, veined, many-puffed clouds. More than 8 parts: yes.

Changed: Dropped the village, cypresses, and the bushes and trees across the middle ground. Merged the clouds into four or five soft masses and the mountains into two silhouettes. Turned the lavender into rows of loose dabs, darker at the base.

Why: A 14x11 canvas at beginner level can't hold a village or single stalks, and the last balloon lesson jumped from flat rows to thousands of stalks.

A sunset scene in three bands: a hot orange-and-coral sky with the sun just left of center, a band of purple mountains and golden hills with one tree, and a lavender field whose rows and two paths all run to one point. The balloon is the subject, but the lavender rows are the hard part: they're a dense texture that has to be built in passes, and their perspective lines have to stay straight from the block-in to the finish.

Subject: A striped hot air balloon floating over rows of lavender at sunset, with a lone tree on a golden hill
Focal point: The striped balloon, upper left (center 28% across, 15% down in the frame)
Light: The setting sun, low and a little left of center (43% across, 41% down in the frame), shining toward the viewer: the balloon's right side, the tree's left side, and the tops of the lavender rows catch the light

What it saw, back to front

  1. sunset sky gradient and sun
  2. coral clouds
  3. far purple mountains, blue ridge, and lake glint
  4. golden and olive rolling hills
  5. lone tree on the right hill
  6. lavender field rows and the two dirt paths
  7. hot air balloon
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

The owner named acrylic-paint-along-beginner.

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint along, back to front, fits a landscape like this exactly: sky first, then far mountains, hills, tree, the field, and the balloon last on top of the finished sky.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

It starts on a toned ground with a sketch and a flat block-in of the whole picture; the owner paints YouTube-style paint-alongs on white canvas, and this picture's sky-to-field order is the paint-along order anyway.

How the paint recipes were worked out24 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order11 steps

Back to front: the sky runs past the hills so they go over it, then clouds, mountains and lake, hills, the tree on its hill, the lavender in three passes over the whole field (flat rows, mid tufts, light tops), then the balloon's stripes, its shading and basket, and the last highlights.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky and the sun

    The whole background in one wet blend, so the clouds and everything else sit on it.

  2. 2. Paint the coral clouds

    Clouds go on the dry sky with three values, before anything in front of them.

  3. 3. Paint the far mountains and the lake

    The farthest land: soft, flat, no texture, with the lake glint in the valley.

  4. 4. Paint the golden hills

    The middle ground, over the bottom of the sky, so the tree has a crest to stand on.

  5. 5. Paint the lone tree

    On the dry hill, before the lavender in front of it.

  6. 6. Block in the lavender rows and paths

    Flat rows and paths first, so the perspective is set before any texture.

  7. 7. Dab the lavender bodies

    First texture pass over the whole field, so no area jumps from flat to dense.

  8. 8. Dab the light lavender tops

    Second texture pass: only the lit tops.

  9. 9. Paint the balloon's stripes

    The subject goes on the finished sky, flat first.

  10. 10. Shade the balloon and add the basket

    Shadow on the side away from the sun, then the basket hanging below.

  11. 11. Add the brightest highlights

    The brightest highlights last, on the balloon's sunlit side and the front tufts.

Where Claude drew diagrams4 steps, free

Three steps build shapes a beginner can't start from a picture alone: the tree's Y and clumps, the field's perspective lines, and the balloon's outline. The tufts got a diagram too, from the step review. The rest are gradients, flat bands, or one repeated mark.

  • Step 5: Paint the lone tree beginner check

    Noticed: The trunk forks into a Y inside the crown, and the crown is a clumpy ball; where the branches start isn't clear from the picture.

    Pieces: A trunk, a Y of two branches, one big round crown, then clumps around its edge, with light dabs on the sun side.

  • Step 6: Block in the lavender rows and paths beginner check

    Noticed: Every row and both paths aim at one point; placing the lines takes more than a sentence.

    Pieces: A dot, two path wedges from it, then row lines fanning out, wider toward the front.

  • Step 7: Dab the lavender bodies step review (6b), 2026-11-11

    Noticed: The step review asked to see one patch built tuft by tuft, since flicked tufts over a dark base are hard to picture.

    Pieces: The dark row and its navy gap, then tufts flicked up from the base, then smaller tufts between with dark still showing.

  • Step 9: Paint the balloon's stripes beginner check

    Noticed: The balloon appears whole in one step, and its stripes have to bow with the shape.

    Pieces: A circle for the top, a tapered piece for the bottom, then stripe curves from the top center down.

What the reviewer caught27 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The finish turned the balloon's dusty teal stripes into a brighter ultramarine. Judged acceptable, not redone, since ultramarine is the palette's blue; a teal mix (ultramarine, a touch of yellow, white) would be closer to the photo.
  • Low-quality step renders don't count rows: a redo with an exact row count kept its own four lines a side. Making the flat block-in from the next step's rows (throwaway filter, then a seeded render) fixed it. A row-flattening filter would belong in tools.py (#11 filter request).
  • The finish step's regions covered the lake, so the backward pass couldn't put the finished lake into earlier steps and one step showed a dull lake. Give the last step regions only for what it adds.
  • Every render stopped the sky about 4% above the 66% line I asked for (at 62%), even after redos. The text uses the measured 62%.
  • A render-step --fix on the mountains filled the white below the ridge with an orange strip rather than the step 1 gold; the hills cover it, so it was left.
  • The step pictures' balloon stripes drift between steps 9, 10, and the finish (the step review saw it); lock-steps can't help inside the balloon's own region. Not redone; the finish step tells the painter to keep their own stripes.
  • Skill/tool gap: the review subagent for step 6b said PIL wasn't available to it for zooming; it didn't need it, but the skill could tell it to run .venv/Scripts/python.exe for crops.
  • The research notes don't cover lavender rows specifically; the plan used the general 'strokes toward a vanishing point' and 'flicking' results.
